home-remodeling.local_heading: One mile of A1A, held to a higher standard
intro_paragraphs: Golden Beach runs about a mile along A1A with the Atlantic on one side, the Intracoastal on the other, and fewer than 400 single-family homes in between. No condos, no commercial, nowhere to trade up to without leaving town. So owners here remodel deeply instead of moving: cottages from the 1920s founding era, mid-century ranches on Golden Beach Drive and the Parkways, and substantial waterfront houses on Ocean Boulevard and the gated islands all eventually get taken back to structure and rebuilt around how the family actually lives.

Permitting runs through the Town of Golden Beach Building Department, which does things its own way: online submittal, contractor registration with the Town, a first inspection due within days of permit issuance, and larger projects that can go before the Building Regulation Advisory Board. Construction hours are 8:00 am to 6:00 pm, Monday through Friday, never weekends. Because the entire town is a barrier island, flood-zone elevations and FEMA substantial-improvement math shape what an older house can absorb, and every window, door, and roof assembly needs Miami-Dade product approvals.

Over 150 remodels and additions in more than 20 years of South Florida building, and PGX Builders Group pulled a permit for each of them. In Golden Beach that translates to a fixed written scope before the first wall opens, a supervisor on site every working day, and a jobsite kept exactly as the Town requires: fenced, screened, swept, and silent by six. In a town this small, your neighbors will judge us by your driveway. We plan for that.

faqs.q: Do remodels in Golden Beach need approval beyond a building permit?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Beyond the Town-issued permit, contractors must be registered with the Town of Golden Beach, and larger projects or exterior changes can be reviewed by the Building Regulation Advisory Board, which meets on its own calendar rather than on demand. We build that review into the schedule from day one so board dates never become the surprise that stalls your project.

faqs.q: What are the construction rules like in Golden Beach?
faqs.a: Strict, and we think that is fair. Work runs 8:00 am to 6:00 pm, Monday through Friday only, with no construction on weekends or Town holidays. Sites must be fenced with tight wind screens, dumpsters covered nightly, streets swept, and crews parked off the roadway, since curb parking is not allowed. PGX runs every jobsite to those standards as a baseline, not a stretch goal.

faqs.q: Should I remodel my Golden Beach house or tear it down?
faqs.a: It depends on the structure, the elevation, and what you want to keep. A deep remodel can preserve an existing footprint and character while replacing everything that matters, and it often makes sense when the bones are sound. When flood elevation or foundation issues stack up, rebuilding can win. We walk the house, run the numbers both ways, and tell you plainly which side of the line you are on.

faqs.q: How does the FEMA substantial-improvement rule affect my remodel?
faqs.a: On a barrier island like Golden Beach it matters. If the cost of improvements crosses the regulatory threshold relative to your structure's value, the home can be required to meet current flood elevation standards, which changes the entire project. We model that math during design, not after permitting, so you decide the scope with full information instead of discovering the rule mid-project.

faqs.q: What is a realistic budget for remodeling a Golden Beach home?
faqs.a: There is no honest one-line answer, and we will not pretend otherwise. Scope, structural changes, and finish level drive the number, and Golden Beach projects tend toward custom millwork, stone, and full impact glazing, which puts them at the serious end of Miami remodeling budgets. What we do promise: a fixed written scope, itemized pricing before demolition, and no invented change orders.

kitchen-remodeling.local_heading: The room that hosts a whole town
intro_paragraphs: In a town with no restaurants, no commercial strip, and a private beach, the kitchen carries more weight than usual. Golden Beach entertaining happens at home, and the kitchens in houses on Ocean Boulevard, the gated islands, and the avenues like Terracina and Massini are expected to feed a holiday crowd without breaking character. The common project: a compartmentalized 1960s or 1980s kitchen opened to the living space, rotated toward the water, and rebuilt around an island that seats everyone who wanders in.

Even an interior kitchen remodel pulls permits through the Town of Golden Beach Building Department once plumbing, electrical, or structure moves, and the Town's small Building Department runs on its own unhurried cadence, so a well-run schedule matters more here than in most of Miami. Logistics matter too: A1A is the only road through town, curb parking is prohibited, and roadways cannot be blocked, which means slab and cabinet deliveries get choreographed, not improvised. If your project touches windows or doors, the glass needs Miami-Dade product approvals for the hurricane zone.

PGX approaches a Golden Beach kitchen the way a millwork shop would: shop drawings approved before demolition, stone templated after cabinets are set, appliances relocated with proper gas, venting, and power rather than clever workarounds. The rest of your house stays sealed off and clean while we work, one PGX supervisor answers for the site daily, and the scope you signed is the scope we build. That is the whole trick, and almost nobody does it.

faqs.q: Does a kitchen remodel in Golden Beach require a permit?
faqs.a: If the project moves plumbing, electrical, gas, or structure, yes, and most serious kitchens move all four. Permits go through the Town of Golden Beach Building Department, which uses online submittal and keeps compact counter hours. That rhythm rewards contractors who plan inspections in advance and punishes the ones who call the morning of. We schedule around it from the start.

faqs.q: How do deliveries work when there is no street parking?
faqs.a: Carefully. The Town prohibits parking along its curbs and does not tolerate blocked roadways, so PGX arranges crew parking off the street and schedules stone, cabinetry, and appliance deliveries in tight windows with the site cleared to receive them. When a truck must stage on a roadway, the Town's rules require a certified flagman or a Town officer, and we arrange that rather than gamble on a citation.

faqs.q: Can you open my kitchen to the water view?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Most Golden Beach kitchens were designed decades ago as sealed work rooms, and the wall between the kitchen and the living or dining space is often structural. We have an engineer size the beam, pull the permit, and open the room so the person cooking finally sees the pool, the dock, or the ocean instead of a backsplash.

faqs.q: What cabinet materials hold up near the ocean?
faqs.a: Salt air and humidity are relentless a block from the Atlantic, so we specify marine-tolerant construction: quality plywood boxes rather than bare MDF in wet zones, sealed finishes on every face, and hardware that resists corrosion. Painted and high-pressure laminate finishes behave well here, and natural wood works when it is finished on all six sides. We choose materials for the climate first, the catalog second.

faqs.q: What should I budget for a kitchen remodel in Golden Beach?
faqs.a: Custom cabinetry, natural stone, and appliance relocation put most of our Golden Beach kitchens well into six figures, and we would rather say that plainly than lure anyone in with a teaser number. The written proposal breaks out cabinetry, stone, appliances, and construction separately, so you can see where the money goes and adjust the scope before we start, not after.

bathroom-remodeling.h1: Bathrooms that shrug off salt air
bathroom-remodeling.hero_sub: Primary suites, frameless showers, and stone baths for Golden Beach homes, waterproofed like the ocean is a block away, because it is. Permitted, inspected, and supervised daily under Lic. CGC1539072.
bathroom-remodeling.local_heading: Baths built a block from the Atlantic
intro_paragraphs: The bathrooms in Golden Beach houses rarely match the rest of the property. A home on North Island or Golden Beach Drive may have a renovated kitchen and a serious pool while the primary bath is still a compartmentalized relic from whenever the house was built, with a step-in tub nobody uses. The remodel owners actually want combines those small rooms into one true suite: a frameless shower with room to move, a freestanding tub, stone underfoot, and morning light that does not come from a fixture.

Moving fixtures means opening the slab in most of these houses, and that means permits through the Town of Golden Beach Building Department, with rough plumbing and electrical inspected before anything closes up. The Town inspects methodically and to its own calendar, so sequencing the trades correctly is the difference between a five-week bath and a five-month one. Coastal humidity raises the stakes on ventilation and vapor control, and any new glazing in a shower or above a tub needs impact-rated, Miami-Dade approved product.

Waterproofing is where PGX earns its reputation, precisely because it is invisible at the walk-through. Every shower we build in Golden Beach gets a full membrane system and a flood test before a single tile goes on, and we photograph what gets buried so you have proof, not promises. One supervisor runs the site daily, floors and finishes outside the work zone stay protected, and the written scope covers fixtures down to the model number.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to remodel a bathroom in Golden Beach?
faqs.a: For anything beyond swapping a faucet, yes. Relocating fixtures, opening the slab, changing electrical, or altering a window all require permits through the Town of Golden Beach Building Department, and the Town inspects roughs before walls close. Unpermitted bath work tends to surface at resale in a town where buyers do their homework, so doing it right the first time is cheaper than doing it twice.

faqs.q: How long does a primary bathroom remodel take here?
faqs.a: A full gut with slab plumbing changes typically runs a few months from demolition to final inspection, and honesty requires saying the Town's careful inspection process adds structure to that timeline. The schedule lives or dies on sequencing: plumbing and electrical roughs, inspections, waterproofing, flood test, then tile. We publish the sequence in the proposal so you can hold us to it week by week.

faqs.q: How do you waterproof showers in a beachfront climate?
faqs.a: With a full membrane system carried up the walls, sloped pans, and sealed penetrations, then a flood test held before tile goes down. Golden Beach adds coastal humidity to the usual physics, so we also spec ventilation that actually exhausts outside and finishes rated for wet, salty air. The materials are ordinary to buy and rare to install correctly, which is the entire difference between builders.

faqs.q: Can I have a window in the shower this close to the ocean?
faqs.a: Yes, and done right it is one of the best features a coastal bathroom can have. The glazing must be impact-rated with a Miami-Dade product approval, set in properly flashed openings, and we typically use obscured or switchable glass for privacy. We detail the sill and surround like the exterior wall it is, because a shower window that leaks does its damage quietly for years.

faqs.q: What does a high-end bathroom remodel cost in Golden Beach?
faqs.a: Less than the kitchen, more than most people guess. Slab plumbing changes, stone, frameless glass, and quality fixtures set the floor, and finish selections move the ceiling. We are a high-end contractor and price accordingly, with an itemized written scope so nothing is vague. If a number matters to you, we would rather engineer the scope to meet it than surprise you later.

home-additions.local_heading: Room to grow on a mile of coastline
intro_paragraphs: Nobody is making more Golden Beach. The town has been built out for decades, the lots are what they are, and a family that outgrows a mid-century floor plan on Golden Beach Drive or Center Island has two choices: leave a town they chose for its guardhouse, private beach, and one-mile calm, or add on. Most add on. Rear extensions push living space toward the pool or the dock, and second-story additions buy bedrooms plus something the flat lots cannot otherwise offer, a view over the rooftops to the water.

Additions here answer to the Town of Golden Beach Building Department and, for larger projects, the Building Regulation Advisory Board. Setbacks and lot coverage set the envelope, and the coastal rules do the rest: structures engineered for High-Velocity Hurricane Zone winds, FEMA substantial-improvement math when the existing house is older, and, on Intracoastal lots, seawall obligations at conforming NAVD-88 elevations that pull in county and state agencies. Projects fronting Ocean Boulevard even need a state lane-closure permit when trucks must stage on A1A. None of this is a problem. All of it is homework.

PGX builds additions structure-first: foundations evaluated before promises are made, tie beams and columns strengthened where a second story demands it, and new roof lines resolved into old ones so the finished house reads as original. You get a fixed written scope, an engineer's numbers instead of a salesman's, and a site run to the Town's exacting conduct rules while your family keeps living in the house. One team owns the job from estimate to warranty.

faqs.q: Will my addition go before the Building Regulation Advisory Board?
faqs.a: Larger projects in Golden Beach can be routed through the Building Regulation Advisory Board in addition to standard permitting, and the board meets on a set schedule rather than whenever a project is ready. We treat board review as a design-phase milestone, preparing drawings that answer the predictable questions the first time, because a clean first presentation is the cheapest schedule insurance available.

faqs.q: What should Intracoastal lot owners know about seawalls?
faqs.a: The Town takes seawalls seriously. Permits on Intracoastal properties come with an owner's obligation to repair or replace a deteriorated seawall to conforming elevations, measured in NAVD-88, under the Town code, with Miami-Dade DERM and state agencies involved where applicable. If your addition heads toward the water side of the lot, we assess the seawall early so its condition informs the budget instead of ambushing it.

faqs.q: Can my house structurally take a second story?
faqs.a: Some can, many need help first. Mid-century Golden Beach homes were built for one story of load in a gentler code era, so the honest path runs through a structural evaluation of the foundation and tie beams before any design work you fall in love with. Where reinforcement is feasible, we price it as part of the real scope. Where it is not, we say so and propose the extension that works.

faqs.q: How do you stage a major addition on Ocean Boulevard?
faqs.a: By the book, because the book here is specific. Ocean Boulevard is state road A1A, so staging trucks there requires a lane-closure permit from FDOT, and the Town requires a certified flagman or Town officer whenever concrete pours put vehicles on its roads. Heavy equipment cannot be stored on site overnight without a special exception. We build all of that into the construction plan and price it upfront.

faqs.q: How long does a home addition take in Golden Beach?
faqs.a: Design and engineering typically run a few months, Town review adds its own rhythm, and construction on a substantial addition is measured in many months, not weeks, especially with the Town's Monday-through-Friday work hours. Anyone quoting a dramatically faster schedule is planning to disappoint you politely. We commit to a sequenced timeline in writing and report progress against it every week.

outdoor-living.local_heading: Outdoor living where the beach is private
intro_paragraphs: Golden Beach is a town organized around being outside: a private beach with a pavilion dating to 1924, docks off the island streets, and backyards that face either sunrise over the Atlantic or sunset across the Intracoastal. Ocean Boulevard has been famous for outdoor living since Eric Clapton put one of its addresses on an album cover in 1974. Owners here invest in covered terraces, summer kitchens, pool surrounds, and motor courts because in this climate the backyard is not seasonal, it is the largest room in the house.

Exterior work still means permits through the Town of Golden Beach Building Department, and the Town's construction standards follow you outdoors: sites fenced and screened, streets swept, pools under construction kept treated, and any damage a contractor causes to Town curbs or roadways repaired at the contractor's expense. Structures like pergolas and summer kitchens get engineered for hurricane-zone wind loads, dock and seawall work on the Intracoastal side brings Miami-Dade DERM and state agencies into the conversation, and oceanfront lots can trigger state coastal construction rules. We flag all of it before design, not during construction.

The PGX difference outdoors is specification discipline. Salt spray destroys optimistic material choices within two summers, so we build with marine-grade stainless, sealed stone and porcelain, and finishes rated for coastal exposure, then coordinate stucco, paint, re-roofing, and impact openings so the whole exterior reads as one decision. A written fixed scope covers it all, a PGX supervisor checks the site every working day, and the crew conducts itself like a guest in a very quiet town.

faqs.q: Do outdoor projects in Golden Beach need permits?
faqs.a: Almost all of them. Summer kitchens, pergolas, terraces, driveways, and anything structural or with utilities runs through the Town of Golden Beach Building Department, and outdoor structures must be engineered for High-Velocity Hurricane Zone wind loads. The Town also enforces jobsite standards outdoors, from covered dumpsters to swept streets. Skipping permits on exterior work is especially visible in a town with its own police force and attentive neighbors.

faqs.q: What applies to work on oceanfront lots?
faqs.a: Oceanfront parcels carry an extra layer: work near the dune line can fall under state coastal construction rules in addition to Town permitting, and staging vehicles on Ocean Boulevard, which is state road A1A, requires an FDOT lane-closure permit. None of this makes a terrace or pool surround impossible. It makes early due diligence valuable, which is why we confirm the regulatory picture before drawings are finished.

faqs.q: Which outdoor materials actually survive salt air?
faqs.a: The ones specified for marinas, not patios. We use 316 stainless steel hardware and appliances, dense porcelain pavers or properly sealed stone, powder-coated aluminum over ferrous metals, and coastal-rated paints and sealers on stucco and wood. Tropical hardwoods and quality composites both perform well on decks and ceilings. The premium over standard materials is real but modest compared to rebuilding a corroded summer kitchen in year three.

faqs.q: Will construction tear up my street or my neighbor's?
faqs.a: Not on our jobs, and in Golden Beach it cannot: the Town holds contractors financially responsible for damage to its curbs, gutters, and roadways, prohibits parking along the curbs, and expects sites swept clean at least twice a day. We stage deliveries in scheduled windows, keep crews parked off the street, and use a certified flagman when trucks must move on Town roads. Your neighbors should barely notice us.

faqs.q: Can you coordinate a re-roof with an outdoor renovation?
faqs.a: Yes, and sequencing them together is usually smarter than doing them apart. Roofing, stucco, paint, impact openings, and terrace structures share flashing lines and scaffolding, so combining them avoids paying twice for access and prevents the classic mistake of a new terrace scarred by a later roof tear-off. We schedule the roof first, protect it, then build beneath it in the right order.

permitting-compliance.local_heading: How permits work in a one-mile town
intro_paragraphs: Golden Beach has no condominiums and no commercial strip: under 400 single-family houses and one road running through them. The houses have been remodeled in rounds since the 1929 founding era. A 1950s ranch on South Parkway gets a new roof, a Terracina Avenue house gets re-glazed with impact windows, an Ocean Boulevard estate rebuilds its seawall, a pool deck on Center Island comes out and goes back. Every one of those rounds should have left behind a permit that reached final inspection. Some did not, and the gap surfaces years later, on somebody else's calendar.

The authority is the Town of Golden Beach Building Department, which stamps nothing out of habit. Contractors must be registered with the Town before a permit is issued, and the company qualifier signs the application and the owner's affidavit. Submittals go through the Town's online system, counter service by appointment. Larger projects and new construction go before the Building Regulation Advisory Board, which meets on its own calendar. This is the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone, so openings and roofing need a Miami-Dade Notice of Acceptance or Florida Product Approval, and on a barrier island FEMA substantial-improvement limits can reshape a project before it starts.

PGX Builders Group has spent more than twenty years building in South Florida, with over 150 remodels and additions delivered and a permit pulled for every one. On a compliance job that experience is mostly sequencing: drawings, engineering and product documentation assembled before anything is filed, review comments answered by us rather than handed back to you, inspections requested only when the work will actually pass, and a written record you can put in front of a title company later. Lic. CGC1539072 stays on the file from the first application to the last sign-off. We do not get around requirements. We make meeting them uneventful.

faqs.q: My lien search came back with an unclosed permit on the house. What now?
faqs.a: It came out of the municipal lien and permit search your buyer's title company runs, and lenders rarely fund around one. You do not need the original contractor. A licensed contractor can take the file over, pull the Town's records, find which inspections were never called, open or test the work where it is hidden, correct what fails, and carry it to final. Start the day you find it, not the week of closing.

faqs.q: Who issues building permits in Golden Beach, the Town or Miami-Dade County?
faqs.a: The Town of Golden Beach runs its own building department and issues the permit. Contractors must be registered with the Town first, and the company qualifier is the one who signs the permit application. Miami-Dade still appears in the file through product approvals, and county and state agencies join the conversation on seawall, dock and oceanfront work.

faqs.q: What actually needs a permit on a house like mine?
faqs.a: More than most owners expect. Structural changes, electrical, plumbing, mechanical, window and door replacement, roofing, pools, generators, seawalls and docks all require one, and window and door work drags Miami-Dade approved products in with it. The work that quietly skips a permit here is usually the small stuff: an air conditioning changeout, a rebuilt pool deck, a garage turned into a gym. Those are exactly the items a lien search finds later.

faqs.q: Does 40-year recertification or a milestone inspection apply to my Golden Beach house?
faqs.a: No. Miami-Dade's building recertification program exempts single-family homes, and Florida's milestone inspection and structural integrity reserve study rules apply to condominium and cooperative buildings of three or more habitable stories. Golden Beach is single-family only, so it has neither. What carries the risk here instead is your own permit history, along with flood elevation and FEMA substantial-improvement rules. If you also own a condo residence in Sunny Isles or Aventura, that is a separate conversation, and one we have often.

faqs.q: What does it cost to clean up a permit problem, and how long does it take?
faqs.a: Both depend on what the record shows. Closing a permit where the work is sound and only a final inspection was skipped is a modest exercise. Closing one where a wall has to be opened, or an engineer has to certify what is already built, is a project. Time runs in weeks rather than days, longer when board review or new drawings are involved. Fees are set by the Town and the county, and we pass them through. We price it after we read the file.
